claimsToVerify: Roman school days typically began before dawn.
Wealthy children were accompanied to school by an enslaved paedagogus carrying lanterns or books.
Elementary schooling often took place in rented shop spaces, pergolas, or public colonnades rather than dedicated school buildings.
Wax tablets (tabulae) and styluses were standard tools for writing practice.
Calculi (pebbles) and counting boards were standard for elementary arithmetic.
Corporal punishment with canes (ferulae) or rods was standard and documented by Roman authors like Horace and Martial.
Most Roman children who received formal schooling concluded around age eleven or twelve before entering apprenticeships or work.
Advanced rhetoric education was largely reserved for the wealthy elite pursuing political and legal careers.
